marking: 1 mark per correct answer; raw score out of 40 is converted to a band (whole or half band). Published reference points: about 16/40 = band 5, 23/40 = band 6, 30/40 = band 7, 35/40 = band 8. The same Listening test is taken by Academic and General Training candidates.
general_rules: Four parts with 10 questions each. Each recording is heard ONCE only.
Questions come in the same order as the information in the recording.
Parts 1 and 2 are everyday social situations; Parts 3 and 4 are educational and training situations. Difficulty rises from Part 1 to Part 4.

A range of accents is used, including British, Australian, New Zealand and North American (regional varieties such as Scottish, Irish or Canadian fall within these). Mix accents across a test; one speaker keeps one accent.

Paper-based: candidates write on the question paper while listening, then get 10 minutes at the end to transfer answers to the answer sheet. Computer-delivered: answers are typed during the recording, with 2 minutes at the end to review them and no transfer time.
Before each question block the recording gives a pause to read the questions, and each part ends with a short pause to check answers.
recorded_frame: First, you have some time to look at Questions {from} to {to}.
Now listen carefully and answer Questions {from} to {to}.
Before you hear the rest of the {conversation/talk}, you have some time to look at Questions {from} to {to}.
Now listen and answer Questions {from} to {to}.
That is the end of Part {n}. You now have some time to check your answers to Part {n}.
That is the end of the Listening test. You now have ten minutes to transfer your answers to the Listening answer sheet. (paper-based only)

sections.context: Everyday social situation: a conversation between two speakers, usually a transactional exchange (phone or face-to-face), e.g. making travel arrangements, booking accommodation, a course or an event, joining a club, hiring equipment, reporting a lost item, enquiring about a job or service.
format_notes: Easiest part; mostly factual detail: names (often spelt out letter by letter), numbers (phone, reference, postcode), dates, times, prices, addresses, days, quantities and simple nouns.
Usually split into two blocks (e.g. Questions 1–6 and 7–10) with a reading pause before each; occasionally one block of 10.
A completion task is almost always present; typical limit 'ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER'.
One speaker (e.g. the caller) asks and the other gives information; answers usually come from the information-giver, and the form follows the order of the conversation.

sections.speakers: 1 (one main speaker; sometimes briefly introduced by a second speaker such as a radio presenter)
sections.context: Everyday social situation: a monologue, e.g. a talk about local facilities, a guided tour, a radio item about a community event, an orientation talk for new volunteers, members or staff, information about a festival, park or sports centre.
format_notes: Usually two blocks of different types (e.g. Questions 11–15 multiple choice, 16–20 map labelling).
Map or plan labelling is most common here: the speaker walks through a site using direction and position language.
The speaker signposts the stages of the talk ('Let me start with…', 'Moving on to…', 'Finally…').

sections.speakers: 2 main speakers (occasionally 3, e.g. two students with a tutor)
sections.context: Educational or training situation: a conversation, e.g. two students planning an assignment, presentation or research project; a student and tutor discussing feedback, a course choice or fieldwork; trainees evaluating a placement.
format_notes: Questions often target opinions, attitudes, agreement or disagreement, decisions, and what each speaker thinks about something, not just facts.
Speakers suggest, question, reject and revise ideas, so most options are mentioned and distractors are plentiful.
Usually two blocks; multiple choice with three options (A–C) and matching (e.g. opinion A–G to each item) are typical.

sections.context: Academic subject: a monologue such as a university lecture or a student's presentation (e.g. a topic in biology, history, psychology, engineering, business or environmental science).
format_notes: Hardest part: denser academic vocabulary and longer, more complex sentences.
Usually one continuous talk with no pause in the middle; candidates look at all the questions before it starts (the reading pause may be longer than for other parts).
Most often a single note-completion block of all 10 questions under sub-headings that mirror the lecture's structure; the limit is often 'ONE WORD ONLY'.
Answers are usually nouns or noun phrases; the lecture signposts each new sub-topic.

rubric_placeholders.{from}: first question number of the block (Part 1: 1–10, Part 2: 11–20, Part 3: 21–30, Part 4: 31–40 in a full test; a standalone practice section may number from 1)
rubric_placeholders.{to}: last question number of the block
rubric_placeholders.{count_word}: how many answers to choose, in capitals, e.g. 'FIVE' or 'TWO'
rubric_placeholders.{stem_question}: the matching question line, e.g. 'What does the speaker say about each of the following …?' or 'Which feature does each area have?'

word_limit_phrases: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER
NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER
answer_conventions: Spelling must be correct: a misspelt answer scores 0 (no partial credit). Names spelt out letter by letter in the recording must be copied exactly.
British and American spellings are both accepted (e.g. colour/color, metre/meter, programme/program).
Upper or lower case both acceptable; writing all answers in capitals is allowed.
Numbers may be written as digits or words; digits are recommended. Under 'AND/OR A NUMBER' limits a number does not count as a word.

Dates, times and prices may be written in any clear standard form (e.g. 15 March / March 15 / 15th March; 7.30 / 7:30 pm; £25 / 25 pounds). A unit or symbol printed next to the gap does not need to be written again.
Exceeding the word limit makes the answer wrong, even if the correct word is included. Hyphenated words count as one word; contracted forms are not tested.
Answers must fit the gap grammatically (e.g. singular/plural as heard); words are written as heard, not changed in form.
In answer keys, optional words appear in brackets and alternatives are separated by a slash; two gaps that ask for a pair of items may be accepted 'in either order'.
Letter answers (multiple choice, matching, map labelling): write only the letter. MULTIPLE_CHOICE_MULTI letters may be given in either order; each question number is worth one mark.

Paper-based: answers are first written on the question paper and then copied during the 10-minute transfer; errors made while copying (e.g. spelling) are marked wrong. Computer-delivered: answers are typed directly and there is only a 2-minute review.
script_conventions: Answers are heard in question order, and each answer is stated clearly once. Leave natural talk (8–20 seconds of speech) between consecutive answers so candidates can write; never put two answers in the same short clause.

Completion answers are the exact words spoken, while the text around each gap paraphrases the recording (a synonym or restructured sentence), so candidates must listen for meaning, not matching words.

Distractors: mention a plausible wrong value before the right one and then correct it ('It's on the 13th… no, sorry, the 14th'); give several numbers or times with only one answering the question (old vs new price, adult vs child fee); make every multiple-choice option heard but only one match the question; have one speaker suggest something the other rejects; replace a plan ('we were going to… but in the end…').

Signposting: monologues (Parts 2 and 4) mark their stages ('First of all…', 'Moving on to…', 'Another important point…', 'To sum up…'); signposting helps candidates keep their place but never gives the answer itself.

Part 1 realism: the information-giver spells names and unusual words ('That's H-A-R-T-L-E-Y'), reads out phone and reference numbers in groups, confirms details, and uses fillers and back-channelling (right, OK, let me see).
Part 3 realism: speakers interrupt, agree, disagree, hedge and change their minds; attitude and opinion questions depend on stance markers (I'm not convinced…, that's a fair point, but…).
Part 4 is a formal but spoken lecture: definitions, examples, causes and effects, research findings and a clear structure that matches the note-completion headings.

Map and plan scripts use direction language consistently from one stated starting point (the entrance, 'you are here'): opposite, next to, just past, at the far end, turn left, in the corner, beside the car park.
Scripts must sound natural: contractions, fillers and discourse markers, but no long irrelevant chat. The accent and gender of each speaker are specified for audio generation.
Recordings are heard once: information needed for an answer must not rely on something mentioned only much earlier, and no answer may be given only by implication.

FORM_COMPLETION.answer_format: Words and/or a number as heard, within the word limit.
FORM_COMPLETION.what_it_tests: Recording factual details a listener would naturally write down (names, addresses, numbers, dates, requirements).
design_rules: A form with a title and labelled fields (e.g. Name, Address, Date of arrival, Special requirements); some fields pre-filled, sometimes one filled in as an example.
Gaps follow the order of the conversation; include at least one spelt-out name and one number.
Typical limit: ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER.

NOTE_COMPLETION.answer_format: Words and/or a number as heard, within the word limit.
NOTE_COMPLETION.what_it_tests: Following the main points and how they relate to each other, and writing down key information.
design_rules: Notes have a title, sub-headings and dash/bullet lines in note style (articles and verbs often dropped).
In Part 4 the sub-headings mirror the lecture's structure; one gap per line at most; usually nouns.
Paraphrase the surrounding note text; the gap word is said exactly.

TABLE_COMPLETION.answer_format: Words and/or a number as heard, within the word limit.
TABLE_COMPLETION.what_it_tests: Recording information that falls into clear categories (e.g. place / time / price / notes).
design_rules: Columns are categories and rows are items discussed in turn; gaps numbered left-to-right, top-to-bottom, matching the order they are heard.
Cells are in note style; some filled in to guide the listener.

FLOW_CHART_COMPLETION.answer_format: Words as heard within the word limit, or one letter per gap from a box of options.
FLOW_CHART_COMPLETION.what_it_tests: Following the stages of a process or procedure described in the recording.
design_rules: Boxes linked by arrows in process order, with the process described in that order.
Box variant: more options than gaps (2–3 extra), options paraphrase what is said.

SUMMARY_COMPLETION.answer_format: Words as heard within the word limit, or one letter per gap.
SUMMARY_COMPLETION.what_it_tests: Understanding the gist and key details of a stretch of speech summarised in continuous prose.
design_rules: A connected paragraph with a title; gaps in the order heard; the summary paraphrases the recording.

SENTENCE_COMPLETION.answer_format: Words and/or a number as heard, within the word limit.
SENTENCE_COMPLETION.what_it_tests: Identifying key information, including relationships such as cause and effect.
design_rules: Each sentence summarises one point of the recording with one gap; the completed sentence must be grammatical.
Typical limits: ONE WORD ONLY or NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS.

MULTIPLE_CHOICE.rubric_template:
Questions {from}–{to}
Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
rubric_variants:
Questions {from} and {to}
Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
MULTIPLE_CHOICE.what_it_tests: Detailed understanding of specific points or general understanding of the main points.
design_rules: Three options A–C (Listening uses three, unlike Reading's four); the stem is a question or an unfinished sentence.
All three options should be mentioned or implied in the recording; only one answers the question. Paraphrase the correct option.
Usually 3–6 questions per block.

MULTIPLE_CHOICE_MULTI.rubric_template:
Questions {from} and {to}
Choose TWO letters, A–E.
MULTIPLE_CHOICE_MULTI.answer_format: One distinct letter per question number; letters accepted in either order.
MULTIPLE_CHOICE_MULTI.what_it_tests: Picking out several relevant points from a longer stretch of speech.
design_rules: Stem after the rubric: 'Which TWO … ?'; five options A–E for two answers.
Every option should be mentioned in the recording; the wrong ones are rejected, used for something else, or not quite what the question asks.
The pair of question numbers sits in sequence with neighbouring blocks, but the two correct options may be heard in either order.

MATCHING.answer_format: One option letter per numbered item.
MATCHING.what_it_tests: Listening for detail, following a conversation, and recognising how facts relate (e.g. which opinion, feature or person goes with each item).
design_rules: Numbered items (e.g. places, people, course options) are discussed in the order listed; options in a box A–G or so.

'Choose FIVE answers from the box' style: more options than items (2–3 extra), each used once. 'You may choose any letter more than once' style: a short fixed scale (e.g. A He'll definitely do it / B He may do it / C He won't do it).
Each item's discussion should mention at least one wrong option as a distractor.

MAP_LABELLING.answer_format: One letter per place (from letters marked on the map or options in a box), or words as heard for the word-limit variant.
MAP_LABELLING.what_it_tests: Understanding a description of a place and how it relates to the visual, and following explanations of where things are and directions.
design_rules: The map/plan shows a clear starting point, some labelled landmarks and more lettered positions than questions (2–3 extra).
Numbered questions are place names, in the order the speaker describes them.
Directions are unambiguous from the stated viewpoint; each answer location should be mentioned with a nearby distractor location.

SHORT_ANSWER.answer_format: Words and/or a number as heard, within the word limit.
SHORT_ANSWER.what_it_tests: Listening for concrete facts such as places, prices or times.
design_rules: Wh-questions paraphrasing the recording; one fact per question.
A question may ask for a list of two or three items, each taking its own question number.

DIAGRAM_LABEL_COMPLETION.answer_format: Words as heard within the word limit, or one letter per label from a box of options.
DIAGRAM_LABEL_COMPLETION.what_it_tests: Understanding a spoken description of a piece of equipment, a structure or a process and relating it to a diagram.
design_rules: The speaker describes the parts in a logical spatial order (top to bottom, input to output) that matches the question order.
Some parts are already labelled to orient the listener.
